Learn from the person's choices

By v/hNovember 24, 2026Note

Originally shared
on LinkedIn

View the post ↗← All journal entries

If a lamp turns itself off at ten, that doesn't mean you chose ten.

Suppose someone usually switches a lamp off near ten. Once the lamp starts helping automatically, its own switch-offs must not count as fresh evidence of the person's preference.

Otherwise, repeating the same action could make a tentative guess look like a stronger habit. Leaving an automatic action uncorrected is also weaker evidence than deliberately using the switch.

For the lamp we're designing, learning should distinguish between a person using the control, an automatic action and a person correcting that action. The distinction belongs inside the lamp. Nobody should have to label their behavior or manage a training screen.

A useful development check would replay a routine with no new manual choices. The lamp should not become more certain about a preferred time merely because it keeps repeating its own decision.

No physical prototype has been built yet. We still need to validate the proposed learning requirement.
